Assuming that the thing hunts because it needs to eat, then feeding a contained skip is just standard procedure for the Foundation. The goal is to contain it and preserve it for future study, not neutralize it. That is one of the main and fundamental guiding mindsets of the Foundation.

There are a lot of entries in the database the Foundation could simply kill or destroy, but they don't because that's not their purpose.

item.content:encoded:
I know this is old but, I feel like it doesn't hold up even by series I standards. For one, the containment area seems unnecessarily large. I get that it's a big bird, but how much room does one bird need?

Also, why not tell the farmer the cow had died of natural causes and then picked apart by crows or vultures? I mean, the article just said that the injuries were consistent with bird attacks, and it mentioned that there were no natural predators in the area capable of taking on a deer so making up a story about coyotes attacking a cow makes no sense.

item.content:encoded: I don't know, usually i'd downvote this but I'm scared it'll be deleted. I really love the whole 'normal thing doing what its not meant to' vibe, not every SCP needs to have a spanning narrative or loads of info. It does need a re-write though, maybe something about it laying eggs so suggesting there might be wild specimens or an idea of it being impossible to move from the arch? It might be better if its something the Foundation has to track and re-contain every night because its on a highway that can't be shut down, though "efforts to create a bypass are underway". Making it clockwork could be pretty cool too, giving it a makers mark to suggest that other statues might also be SCP's.

I do like the rest of the article, but the addendum at the end feels very much like a cheap afterthought. "Oh yeah, it also kills humans. Scary!" item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I find myself asking what unauthorized D-class were doing in the (presumably monitored or at least locked) enclosure in the first place, let alone during 'restricted hours.'

Locking the doors to the enclosure between 8:55 p.m. and 6:05 a.m would prevent this kind of thing from happening again, and would cost nothing to implement.

Is the implication that the D-class were somehow "drawn" to the enclosure? If so, this is a perfect opportunity for an Incident Report adding a touch of the human perspective.

Regardless, the preparer of this report should at the very least mention that having the D-class in there was unauthorized, and an investigation is under way to determine how or why they got in there.

item.content:encoded:
Had to -1 this one. Its just a weird thing, doing weird things, and not particularly well written. This is a giant predatory bird next to a motorway, what happens if one day it gets a taste for cars or mopeds? If such an SCP existed then I doubt the Foundation would view it so laxly. I think either the Containment Procedures need to be updated (possibly just apply restraints for the type of bird in the relative size, such as hawking hoods, etc) or the SCP needs to be updated to show why they're allowing it such free rein.

I think a hood on its head and a steel cable welded to its ankle would probably stop it from buggering off. If its truly emulating a hawk it wouldnt want to take off without being able to see.
